teacher_glossary.definition: The systematic organisation of living things into groups based on shared characteristics. Classification enables scientists to identify, name and communicate about organisms consistently. It is purposeful and constructed — different classification systems organise by different criteria depending on the priorities of those who made them.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse classification with simple sorting or listing — grouping organisms by a single surface feature (e.g. colour) without a systematic basis or purpose.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If classification is just sorting, students cannot understand why formal systems like Linnaean taxonomy exist, why classification systems change over time, or why feature selection matters when constructing dichotomous keys.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare classification with everyday sorting (sorting laundry by colour vs organising a library by subject, author, title). Ask: what makes the library system more useful than the laundry sort? What would break if you used colour to organise a library?

sub_terms.definition: A structured framework for organising organisms into groups — such as Linnaean taxonomy or Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander classification systems based on Country.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students treat 'classification system' as interchangeable with the act of classifying — missing that different systems organise by different criteria and reveal different priorities about what matters.
sub_terms.response: Compare two classification systems for the same set of organisms (e.g. Linnaean vs a First Nations system). Ask: what does each system prioritise? What is visible in one that is invisible in the other?

teacher_glossary.definition: The variety of living organisms on Earth, including diversity within species, between species, and of ecosystems. Biodiversity encompasses all kingdoms — plants, animals, fungi, protists and bacteria — not only the organisms most visible to humans.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think biodiversity means 'lots of animals' — limiting it to large, visible animal species and missing plant, fungal, microbial and ecosystem diversity.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If biodiversity is only animal variety, students cannot understand why classification systems must encompass all kingdoms, or why loss of microbial or plant diversity has ecological consequences.
teacher_glossary.response: Present biodiversity examples across all kingdoms — include bacteria, fungi and protists alongside animals and plants. Ask students to identify which environment in a set is most biodiverse, including one rich in microbial diversity.

teacher_glossary.definition: The branch of science concerned with naming, describing and classifying organisms into a hierarchical system of groups based on shared characteristics. The hierarchy is nested — each level sits within a broader group sharing fewer features, from the broadest level (kingdom) to the most specific (species).
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students memorise the hierarchy levels as a list without understanding that each level represents a nested group — organisms in the same genus share more features than organisms in the same phylum because the group is narrower.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If taxonomy is a memorised sequence rather than a nested hierarchy, students cannot explain why classification at different levels reveals different degrees of relatedness. The structural logic that underpins all classification reasoning is lost.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a nested boxes or Russian dolls model showing how each level fits inside the next. Ask students to explain what happens to the number of shared features as you move from kingdom toward species.

sub_terms.definition: The broadest traditional grouping in Linnaean taxonomy. The major kingdoms — animals, plants, fungi, protists and bacteria — are each defined by fundamental differences in cell structure, nutrition and reproduction.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students assign organisms to kingdoms based on superficial resemblance (e.g. coral is a plant because it doesn't move, mushroom is a plant because it grows in soil) rather than defining features of each kingdom.
sub_terms.response: Present organisms that challenge superficial assignment (coral, mushroom, Euglena). Require students to justify placement using defining kingdom features — not appearance or behaviour.

sub_terms.definition: The nested classification system developed by Carl Linnaeus, organising organisms from broadest group (kingdom) to most specific (species): kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students memorise the level names as a sequence without understanding that each level is nested within the one above, representing progressively more shared features.
sub_terms.response: Use a visual nesting model and ask students to explain what happens to shared features at each level. Have them place a familiar organism at every level to see the narrowing.

sub_terms.definition: An organism that does not fit neatly into existing classification categories — such as Euglena (characteristics of both plants and animals) or viruses (debated whether they are living).
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students treat boundary cases as errors in the classification system rather than informative cases that reveal what the system assumes and where its definitions break down.
sub_terms.response: Present a boundary case and ask: what does this organism's difficulty tell us about the rules our classification system uses? What would we need to change to accommodate it?

teacher_glossary.definition: Characteristics of an organism that can be directly seen, measured or detected — such as body covering, number of limbs, leaf shape, or method of locomotion. Observable features are the basis for classification decisions in taxonomy and dichotomous keys.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students select features that are not reliably observable (e.g. diet, habitat, internal anatomy) or not useful for distinguishing organisms (e.g. 'is alive') when classifying or constructing keys.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Unreliable feature selection undermines both taxonomy and key construction. The feature-selection skill identified in N2's hinge_reason is the foundation for all classification tool use — students who cannot identify useful observable features cannot construct functional keys.
teacher_glossary.response: Give students sets of organisms and ask them to rank features from most to least useful for telling organisms apart. Build a class reference list of reliable observable features across kingdoms.

teacher_glossary.definition: A classification tool that uses a series of paired statements based on observable features to identify organisms. At each decision point, the user chooses between exactly two mutually exclusive options, progressively narrowing identification until a single organism is reached.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students follow key steps procedurally — tracing arrows to reach an answer — without understanding the binary decision logic at each step. They cannot explain what observable feature is being checked or why the two options are mutually exclusive.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Procedural key-following without conceptual understanding of binary decision logic produces key constructions that are structurally broken. Students who cannot explain why each decision point works cannot reverse the process to construct their own keys — this is the Node 3 hinge.
teacher_glossary.response: At each decision point, require students to state: 'What observable feature am I checking? What are the two possible outcomes? Why are they mutually exclusive?' before moving to the next step.

sub_terms.definition: A choice between exactly two mutually exclusive options based on a single observable feature — the fundamental logic unit of a dichotomous key.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students construct decision points with overlapping options (e.g. 'big or small' where the boundary is undefined), subjective criteria, or more than two outcomes — breaking the binary structure that makes keys reliable.
sub_terms.response: Before committing a decision to a key, have students test it: can every organism in the set go to exactly one of the two options with no ambiguity? If not, the decision point needs rewriting.

sub_terms.definition: A specific location in a dichotomous key where the user must choose between two options based on an observable feature. Each decision point eliminates organisms that don't match the chosen option, narrowing identification.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students cannot name the observable feature being checked at a decision point — they follow the path mechanically without understanding what each branch tests or why it separates organisms.
sub_terms.response: At every decision point, require the student to state the feature name and both possible outcomes before choosing: 'At this point I am checking [feature]. The two options are [A] and [B].'

teacher_glossary.definition: An observable feature that reliably separates one group of organisms from another — producing a clean binary split where all members of one group share the feature and all members of the other do not. Not all observable features are discriminating: a feature that varies within a group (e.g. colour in many bird species) fails to discriminate.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students select non-discriminating features when constructing keys — features that work for some organisms in the set but not others, or features that overlap between groups, producing keys that misclassify.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Non-discriminating feature selection is the most common cause of broken dichotomous keys. Node 2's hinge_reason identifies feature-selection skill as the bridge between taxonomy knowledge and key construction — without it, key construction in Node 4 fails.
teacher_glossary.response: Have students test proposed features against the full organism set before committing them to a key. Ask: 'Does this feature split the set cleanly into two groups with no exceptions? If not, find a feature that does.'

teacher_glossary.definition: The reassignment of an organism from one taxonomic group to another based on new evidence — such as DNA analysis revealing that organisms previously grouped by appearance are not closely related, or that organisms in different groups share a recent common ancestor.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students describe reclassification as scientists 'changing their minds' or 'getting it wrong' — treating it as evidence that science is unreliable rather than evidence that science self-corrects in response to new data.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If reclassification equals unreliability, students develop a flawed understanding of the nature of science that undermines confidence in all scientific conclusions. The evaluative step — understanding what reclassification reveals about how science works — is explicitly assessed.
teacher_glossary.response: Scaffold the reasoning chain: what was the old classification? What new evidence emerged? What changed? Then ask: does reclassification show science is broken, or that science is working? Require an evidence-based argument.

teacher_glossary.definition: A model showing the interconnected feeding relationships between organisms in an ecosystem. Unlike a food chain, a food web represents multiple overlapping pathways of energy flow, revealing that most organisms have more than one food source and more than one predator.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students draw food webs with arrows pointing from consumer to food source — reversing the direction of energy flow. Arrows in a food web must show the direction energy moves: from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Reversed arrows make every subsequent energy flow and cascade prediction wrong. If arrows point toward food sources, students read the web as 'what eats what' rather than 'where energy flows' — and cannot trace energy loss through trophic levels.
teacher_glossary.response: Explicitly label arrows as 'energy flows to' rather than 'is eaten by.' Have students trace a single energy pathway from producer to top consumer and check that every arrow points in the direction energy travels.

sub_terms.definition: A single linear pathway showing energy flow from one organism to the next — producer to primary consumer to secondary consumer. A simplified model that shows one route through a food web.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think food chains and food webs are interchangeable — missing that a food chain shows only one pathway while a food web shows the interconnected reality. This leads to oversimplified cascade predictions.
sub_terms.response: Compare a food chain and food web for the same ecosystem. Ask: what information is present in the web but missing from the chain? What prediction would you get wrong using only the chain?

teacher_glossary.definition: An organism that makes its own food from non-living sources — typically through photosynthesis using sunlight. Producers are the entry point for energy in almost all food webs and include plants, algae and some bacteria. All energy in a food web traces back to producers.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think producers are only large green plants — missing algae, phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria, which are the dominant producers in aquatic ecosystems.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If producers are only land plants, students cannot explain energy flow in aquatic ecosystems — which contain the majority of Earth's biomass. Aquatic food webs become inexplicable.
teacher_glossary.response: Present food webs from aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems side by side. Ask students to identify the producer in each — the aquatic examples force recognition of non-plant producers.

sub_terms.definition: An organism that obtains energy by eating other organisms. Primary consumers eat producers; secondary consumers eat primary consumers; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students classify consumers by what they 'prefer' to eat rather than by their trophic position — an omnivore that eats both plants and animals gets misplaced because it occupies multiple trophic levels simultaneously.
sub_terms.response: Use a food web to show how the same organism can be a primary consumer (when eating plants) and a secondary consumer (when eating herbivores). Trophic position depends on the pathway, not the organism.

sub_terms.definition: An organism — typically bacteria or fungi — that breaks down dead organic matter, returning nutrients to the soil or water. Decomposers connect to every trophic level because all organisms eventually die and are decomposed.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students omit decomposers from food webs or place them only at the end of a chain — missing that decomposers process dead matter from every trophic level, not just top consumers.
sub_terms.response: Ask students to draw arrows from every organism in a food web to the decomposer. The resulting diagram makes the decomposer's role in nutrient cycling visible at every level.

sub_terms.definition: An organism that eats producers directly — a herbivore. Primary consumers are the first trophic level above producers.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think 'primary' means 'most important' rather than 'first in the energy pathway from producers.'
sub_terms.response: Trace energy from producer through the web and number each step. Primary = first consumer in the chain, secondary = second. The numbering makes the positional meaning clear.

sub_terms.definition: An organism that eats primary consumers — a carnivore or omnivore that obtains energy at least two steps from the producer.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students assume secondary consumers eat only primary consumers, missing that many secondary consumers are omnivores that also eat producers.
sub_terms.response: Present an omnivore in a food web and trace all its feeding pathways. Ask: is this organism a primary consumer, secondary consumer, or both? The answer depends on which pathway you trace.

teacher_glossary.definition: A community of living organisms (biotic factors) interacting with each other and with the non-living components of their environment (abiotic factors). An ecosystem includes all the feeding relationships, energy flows and matter cycles within a defined area.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think an ecosystem is just a place or habitat — a location where organisms live — without recognising that the interactions between organisms and their environment are what define it.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If an ecosystem is just a location, students cannot reason about how changes to one component (abiotic or biotic) cascade through the system. The interaction concept is what makes prediction possible.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare 'habitat' with 'ecosystem' explicitly. A pond is a habitat; the ecosystem includes all organisms in the pond plus their interactions with water temperature, sunlight, dissolved oxygen and each other.

teacher_glossary.definition: The one-way transfer of energy through an ecosystem, beginning with producers capturing sunlight and passing through consumers at each trophic level. Energy is lost as heat at every transfer — it flows through the system but does not cycle back. This distinguishes energy flow from matter cycling.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students conflate energy flow with matter cycling — believing energy cycles through the ecosystem and can be recovered, rather than understanding that energy flows one way and is progressively lost as heat at each trophic level.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The energy/matter conflation produces systematically wrong cascade predictions. Students who think energy cycles predict recovery rather than loss — they expect populations to bounce back rather than decline when energy input is reduced. This error propagates into every prediction task in Nodes 3 and 4.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a side-by-side diagram: energy enters from the sun, passes through trophic levels with loss at each step, and exits as heat (one-way arrow). Matter cycles between organisms and environment (circular arrows). Ask students to label which diagram shows energy and which shows matter.

sub_terms.definition: The approximation that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next — the remaining 90% is lost as heat through life processes. Used to explain why food webs have few trophic levels and why top predators are rare.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students apply the 10% rule mechanically without understanding why energy is lost — they memorise the number without connecting it to the biological reality that organisms use most of their energy for life processes.
sub_terms.response: Ask students to account for where the 90% goes: movement, growth, reproduction, body heat. Then calculate how much energy reaches a tertiary consumer from 10,000 kJ at the producer level — the dramatic reduction makes the rule concrete.

teacher_glossary.definition: The continuous movement of matter (nutrients, water, carbon) through an ecosystem — from the environment into organisms and back again through decomposition, respiration and other processes. Unlike energy, matter is not lost from the system; it cycles repeatedly between living and non-living components.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students conflate matter cycling with energy flow — believing that matter, like energy, is used up and lost at each trophic level rather than cycling back through the ecosystem.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If matter is lost like energy, students cannot explain decomposition, nutrient return or why ecosystems are sustainable over time. The distinction between one-way energy flow and cyclical matter movement is foundational for AC9S9U03 (Carbon Cycle).
teacher_glossary.response: Trace a single carbon atom through a food web: absorbed by a plant during photosynthesis, eaten by a herbivore, released as CO₂ through respiration, reabsorbed by another plant. The atom returns — energy does not.

teacher_glossary.definition: A position in a food web defined by the number of energy transfers from the producer. Producers occupy the first trophic level; primary consumers the second; secondary consumers the third. Each trophic level contains less available energy than the one below it.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students treat trophic levels as fixed categories for organisms rather than positions in an energy pathway — they assign an organism a single trophic level even when it feeds at multiple levels in a food web.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If trophic levels are fixed organism labels, students cannot reason about omnivores or complex food webs where the same organism occupies different trophic positions depending on the pathway. Energy flow calculations become impossible for real ecosystems.
teacher_glossary.response: Present an omnivore in a food web and ask students to identify its trophic level for each feeding pathway. The organism occupies trophic level 2 when eating plants and trophic level 3 when eating herbivores — it is pathway-dependent.

sub_terms.definition: A diagram showing the amount of energy available at each trophic level, with producers at the broad base and top consumers at the narrow peak. The pyramid shape reflects progressive energy loss at each transfer.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students interpret the pyramid as a hierarchy of importance or population size rather than a representation of available energy — they think organisms at the top are 'most important' rather than 'fewest because energy is scarce.'
sub_terms.response: Ask: why is the pyramid wide at the bottom and narrow at the top? Connect each level's width to the amount of energy available, not to importance. Then ask why there are few top predators — the energy explanation makes it concrete.

teacher_glossary.definition: A non-living component of an ecosystem that affects living organisms — such as temperature, water availability, sunlight, soil pH, wind and salinity. Changes to abiotic factors cascade through food webs by affecting producers first, then the consumers that depend on them.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students list abiotic factors correctly but cannot trace how a change to one factor cascades through multiple populations in a food web — they predict only the immediate first-order effect.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Single-step prediction misses the cascade that defines ecosystem response. A drought doesn't just reduce plant growth — it reduces herbivore populations, which reduces predator populations, which may allow other herbivore populations to increase. Missing the cascade means missing the ecosystem-level consequence.
teacher_glossary.response: Scaffold multi-step reasoning: what changes first? What depends on that? What depends on that? Require students to trace at least three steps through a food web before concluding. Use sentence starters: 'This means that... which causes... which leads to...'

teacher_glossary.definition: A living component of an ecosystem that affects other living organisms — such as predators, prey, competitors, parasites, and decomposers. Changes to biotic factors cascade through food webs as the removal or introduction of one species affects every species connected to it.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students predict only the immediate effect of species removal or introduction without tracing the cascade through the full food web — they identify what the removed species ate or was eaten by, but stop there.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Biotic cascade reasoning requires holding the whole food web in mind simultaneously — the same multi-step reasoning skill required for carbon flow in AC9S9U03. Students who stop at first-order effects treat ecosystems as simple chains rather than interconnected webs.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a food web and remove one species. Ask students to predict effects on every connected species, then the species connected to those, tracing at least two steps beyond the immediate effect. Compare predictions with a real trophic cascade case study.

sub_terms.definition: A species introduced to an ecosystem where it did not naturally occur, which disrupts existing food web relationships — often because it has no natural predators in the new ecosystem and outcompetes native species.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students describe invasive species as 'bad animals' without connecting the disruption to specific food web mechanisms — competition for resources, predation on native species, or displacement of existing trophic roles.
sub_terms.response: Construct a food web before and after an invasive species introduction. Ask: what new feeding relationships appear? What existing relationships are disrupted? What populations increase or decrease and why?

teacher_glossary.definition: All the organisms of one species living in a particular area at a particular time. In ecosystem science, population size is what changes when abiotic or biotic factors shift — food web predictions are about population increases, decreases or stability.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse population with community or ecosystem — using 'population' to refer to all organisms in an area rather than all organisms of one species.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If population means all organisms, cascade predictions become incoherent — students cannot track how one species' population change affects another specific species' population. The specificity of 'one species in one area' is what makes predictions testable.
teacher_glossary.response: Give students a food web and ask them to identify three different populations within it. Emphasise: each species in the web is a separate population. The food web shows how populations interact, not how one population works.

teacher_glossary.definition: A chain of population changes triggered by a single change to an abiotic or biotic factor in an ecosystem. The initial change affects one population, which affects populations connected to it in the food web, which in turn affects further populations — the effects cascade through the web.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students describe the initial change and one consequence but do not trace the chain further — they predict first-order effects only, missing the multi-step cascade that reveals the full ecosystem impact.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: First-order-only prediction is the most common reasoning gap in this standard. Real ecosystem responses involve multiple steps — a drought reduces plants, which reduces herbivores, which reduces predators, which may release pressure on other herbivore populations. Stopping at step one misses the systemic response.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a chain-of-reasoning scaffold: Change → First effect → Second effect → Third effect. Require students to complete at least three links before writing their prediction. Provide the food web as a visual reference throughout.

sub_terms.definition: A specific type of cascade effect triggered by a change at the top of the food web — typically the removal or introduction of a top predator — that cascades down through multiple trophic levels.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students describe the trophic cascade event (e.g. wolves removed, elk increased) without tracing the full chain through the food web to vegetation and other species affected by the vegetation change.
sub_terms.response: Use the Yellowstone wolf reintroduction as a case study. Require students to trace effects from wolves → elk → vegetation → riverbank erosion → beaver habitat — the multi-step chain makes the trophic cascade concept concrete.

teacher_glossary.definition: A simplified representation of a real system, designed to help explain, predict or communicate. In science, models deliberately leave out some details to make the system understandable — a food web model represents feeding relationships but omits factors like disease, weather variation and seasonal changes.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think scientific models are physical replicas or exact copies of reality — they do not recognise that models are deliberate simplifications with assumptions, and that what a model leaves out affects the reliability of predictions made from it.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If models are copies, students cannot evaluate their limitations or explain why predictions from models are uncertain. Model evaluation — identifying what is missing and how that affects predictions — is directly assessed at Node 5.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a simple and complex model of the same ecosystem. Ask: what can the simple model predict? What would it get wrong? What does the complex model add? This makes 'limitation' concrete rather than abstract.

teacher_glossary.definition: The spinning of Earth on its own axis, completing one full turn approximately every 24 hours. Rotation causes the cycle of day and night as different parts of Earth's surface face toward or away from the sun.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse rotation with revolution — using the terms interchangeably or believing that Earth's spinning around its axis is the same as its orbit around the sun.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If rotation and revolution are conflated, students cannot correctly assign causes to phenomena — they attribute seasons to rotation or day/night to revolution. The 3D spatial model required for eclipse and season explanations depends on distinguishing these two simultaneous cycles.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a physical model: spin a globe on its axis (rotation = day/night) while walking it around a lamp (revolution = year). Ask students to identify which motion causes day/night and which causes the year — the simultaneous demonstration makes the distinction physical.

sub_terms.definition: The movement of Earth in its orbit around the sun, completing one full orbit approximately every 365.25 days. Revolution combined with axial tilt produces the cycle of seasons.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think revolution means spinning — the everyday meaning of 'revolve' interferes with the astronomical meaning of orbiting around another body.
sub_terms.response: Explicitly contrast: rotation = spin on axis (like a basketball on a finger), revolution = orbit around another body (like running around a track). Have students demonstrate both simultaneously with a model.

teacher_glossary.definition: The angle at which Earth's axis of rotation is tilted relative to its orbital plane — approximately 23.5°. The axis maintains the same orientation in space throughout Earth's orbit, meaning different hemispheres receive more direct sunlight at different points in the orbit. Axial tilt is the cause of seasons.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students know Earth's axis is tilted but cannot connect the tilt to seasonal effects — they state the fact without explaining how a fixed tilt produces changing solar angles as Earth orbits.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Axial tilt is the causal mechanism for seasons. Students who know the tilt exists but cannot explain how it produces seasonal change will default to the distance misconception (seasons caused by proximity to the sun) because it offers a simpler causal story.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a globe with a fixed tilt angle orbiting a lamp. At each quarter-orbit position, ask: which hemisphere is tilted toward the sun? What season does that hemisphere experience? The fixed tilt producing changing effects at different orbital positions is the key insight.

teacher_glossary.definition: The changing appearance of the moon as seen from Earth over a lunar cycle, caused by the changing angle at which sunlight illuminates the moon's surface relative to the observer. The sequence — new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent — repeats approximately every 29.5 days.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students explain moon phases as caused by Earth's shadow falling on the moon — confusing phases with lunar eclipses. In reality, phases are caused by the moon's position relative to Earth and the sun, which changes how much of the illuminated side we can see.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The shadow misconception persists directly into eclipse explanation. Students who think phases are caused by Earth's shadow will explain lunar eclipses as extreme moon phases and cannot distinguish the two phenomena — this is the Node 2 hinge.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a ball and lamp model. Move the ball around a central observer, asking students to draw what they see at each position. The key moment: when the ball is beside the observer, half is lit — but no shadow from the observer falls on it. Phases are about viewing angle, not shadow.

sub_terms.definition: The complete sequence of moon phases from one new moon to the next, taking approximately 29.5 days. The lunar cycle is caused by the moon orbiting Earth, which continuously changes the angle between sun, moon and observer.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students confuse the length of the lunar cycle with individual phase durations — or think each phase lasts one night rather than understanding the continuous transition across approximately 29.5 days.
sub_terms.response: Show a month of real moon phase photographs with dates. Ask students to calculate how many days the full cycle takes and how many days each named phase lasts — the continuous change becomes visible.

teacher_glossary.definition: An event in which one celestial body passes into the shadow of another, temporarily blocking light. Eclipses require precise alignment of the sun, moon and Earth. They do not occur every month because the moon's orbital plane is tilted approximately 5° relative to Earth's orbital plane — alignment only occurs when the moon crosses this plane at the right time.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students cannot explain why eclipses do not occur every month — they understand the alignment required but not the role of the moon's orbital tilt in making that alignment rare.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Eclipse rarity is directly assessed in the success criteria. Without the orbital tilt explanation, students treat eclipses as randomly occurring rather than as predictable events governed by orbital geometry.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a tilted hoop to represent the moon's orbit around a globe. Show that the moon passes above or below the sun-Earth line most months — only when it crosses the line at new moon or full moon does an eclipse occur.

sub_terms.definition: An eclipse in which the moon passes between the sun and Earth, casting a shadow on Earth's surface. The moon blocks sunlight from reaching a small area of Earth. Solar eclipses occur at new moon — but only when the moon's orbital tilt brings it into the sun-Earth line.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think solar eclipses should happen every new moon — they understand the sun-moon-Earth alignment but not why the moon's orbital tilt prevents alignment most months.
sub_terms.response: Model the tilted orbit: at most new moons, the moon passes above or below the sun-Earth line. Only when new moon coincides with the moon crossing the orbital plane does a solar eclipse occur.

sub_terms.definition: An eclipse in which Earth passes between the sun and moon, casting Earth's shadow on the moon. The moon moves into Earth's shadow and appears darkened or reddish. Lunar eclipses occur at full moon — but only when alignment is precise.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students confuse lunar eclipses with moon phases — specifically, they think a lunar eclipse is just an extreme phase caused by Earth's shadow, rather than a distinct event requiring precise orbital alignment.
sub_terms.response: Compare directly: during a normal full moon, Earth's shadow misses the moon (no eclipse). During a lunar eclipse, the alignment is exact and Earth's shadow falls on the moon. The difference is alignment, not phase.

sub_terms.definition: The darkest, central part of a shadow where all direct light from the source is completely blocked. During a solar eclipse, only observers within the umbra see a total eclipse.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students swap umbra and penumbra — calling the lighter outer shadow the umbra and the darker inner shadow the penumbra, or thinking penumbra means 'no shadow at all.'
sub_terms.response: Use a torch and ball to cast a shadow on a wall. Identify the dark centre (umbra) and lighter edge (penumbra). Mnemonic: umbra = umbrella of total darkness at the centre.

sub_terms.definition: The lighter, outer region of a shadow where only part of the light source is blocked. During a solar eclipse, observers in the penumbra see a partial eclipse — some sunlight is still visible around the moon's edge.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think the penumbra is not a shadow at all — rather than understanding it as a region of partial shadow where some but not all light is blocked.
sub_terms.response: In the torch-and-ball model, have students stand in the penumbra region and observe that some light reaches them — it's dimmer, not dark. Partial shadow, not no shadow.

sub_terms.definition: The approximately 5° angle between the moon's orbital plane and Earth's orbital plane around the sun. This tilt is the reason eclipses do not occur every month — most months, the moon passes above or below the sun-Earth line rather than through it.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students learn the orbital tilt fact without connecting it to eclipse frequency — they state that the moon's orbit is tilted but cannot explain how this prevents monthly eclipses.
sub_terms.response: Use a tilted ring around a globe to show the moon's orbit. At each full moon and new moon position, ask: does the moon cross the sun-Earth line this month? The visual makes the connection between tilt and eclipse rarity concrete.

teacher_glossary.definition: The annual cycle of weather and daylight patterns caused by Earth's axial tilt. As Earth orbits the sun, the tilted axis means each hemisphere alternates between being tilted toward the sun (summer — higher solar angle, longer days) and away from it (winter — lower solar angle, shorter days). Seasons are not caused by distance from the sun.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students explain seasons as caused by Earth being closer to the sun in summer and further away in winter — the distance misconception. This is extremely persistent and directly assessed.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The distance misconception produces confidently wrong answers that students defend vigorously. It cannot explain why the Northern and Southern hemispheres experience opposite seasons simultaneously — which is a direct test of understanding. Students who hold this misconception produce systematically wrong season explanations.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: if seasons are caused by distance, why does Australia have summer when the UK has winter — they're the same distance from the sun. The opposite-hemisphere test directly contradicts the distance explanation and forces the tilt explanation.

sub_terms.definition: The angle at which sunlight strikes Earth's surface at a given location. Higher solar angles (sun more directly overhead) concentrate energy on a smaller area, producing more heating. Solar angle varies by latitude and season due to axial tilt.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students can name solar angle as a factor in seasons without connecting it to heating — they state that the angle changes but cannot explain why a higher angle means more heating per unit area.
sub_terms.response: Shine a torch straight down on a surface (high angle — small bright spot) then at a low angle (same light spread over a larger area, dimmer). Ask: which produces more heating per square metre? The torch demonstration makes the angle-heating connection physical.

sub_terms.definition: The number of hours of daylight at a given location, which varies across the year due to axial tilt. The hemisphere tilted toward the sun has longer days; the hemisphere tilted away has shorter days. Day length is the second mechanism (alongside solar angle) by which tilt produces seasons.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students know day length changes across the year but cannot explain why — they describe the pattern without connecting it to axial tilt and Earth's orbital position.
sub_terms.response: Use a globe with a lamp to show how the terminator (day/night boundary) falls at different orbital positions. At the June position, the Southern Hemisphere has more area in darkness — shorter days. At December, it reverses.

sub_terms.definition: One half of Earth, divided by the equator into Northern and Southern hemispheres. The hemispheres experience opposite seasons simultaneously because when one is tilted toward the sun, the other is tilted away.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students do not connect opposite hemispheric seasons to axial tilt — they may know that Australia and the UK have opposite seasons but cannot explain why using the tilt model.
sub_terms.response: Use a globe tilted toward a lamp. Ask students to identify which hemisphere is tilted toward the sun and which is tilted away. Then ask: what season is each experiencing? Rotate the globe to the opposite orbital position and repeat.

teacher_glossary.definition: The regular rise and fall of sea levels caused primarily by the gravitational pull of the moon on Earth's oceans. The moon's gravity pulls water toward it, creating a bulge of higher water (high tide) on the side of Earth facing the moon and a second bulge on the opposite side. As Earth rotates, locations pass through these bulges, experiencing two high tides and two low tides daily.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think tides are caused by the moon 'pushing' water or by wind, rather than by gravitational pull. Or they understand the near-side bulge but cannot explain the far-side bulge.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Tides integrate the lunar cycle, the Earth-moon-sun model and gravitational force into a single explanatory account. Students who cannot explain the gravitational mechanism cannot distinguish spring from neap tides or connect tidal patterns to moon position.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a diagram showing the moon's gravity pulling water toward it on the near side while the far side bulges because it is pulled less strongly than Earth's centre. Connect to the rotation: as Earth spins, a coastal location rotates through both bulges in one day.

sub_terms.definition: Tides with the greatest tidal range (highest high tides, lowest low tides), occurring when the sun, moon and Earth are aligned — at new moon and full moon. The sun's gravitational pull reinforces the moon's, producing larger tidal bulges.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think spring tides occur only in the spring season — confusing the tidal term with the season name. Or they cannot connect spring tides to the specific moon positions (new and full moon) that cause them.
sub_terms.response: Show a diagram of sun-moon-Earth alignment at new moon and full moon. Ask: when the sun and moon pull in the same direction (or directly opposite), what happens to the tidal bulge? The alignment explanation replaces the seasonal confusion.

sub_terms.definition: Tides with the smallest tidal range (least difference between high and low tide), occurring when the sun and moon are at right angles relative to Earth — at first quarter and third quarter moon. The sun's gravitational pull partially counteracts the moon's.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students cannot distinguish neap from spring tides or connect each to the correct moon position — they know two types exist but confuse which alignment produces which effect.
sub_terms.response: Place the neap and spring tide diagrams side by side. Ask: in which arrangement do the sun and moon work together? In which do they work against each other? Label each with the moon phase that produces it.

sub_terms.definition: A graphical representation of predicted tide heights over time for a specific coastal location, showing the cyclic pattern of high and low tides. Tide charts reveal spring and neap cycles when read across a lunar month.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students can read individual high and low points on a tide chart but cannot identify the spring-neap pattern across a month — they read the chart point-by-point rather than recognising the repeating cycle.
sub_terms.response: Give students a month-long tide chart and ask them to mark the highest highs and lowest lows. Then overlay a lunar calendar — the spring tides align with new and full moons, making the pattern visible.

teacher_glossary.definition: The attractive force that a massive object exerts on other objects. In the Earth-sun-moon system, the moon's gravitational pull on Earth's oceans is the primary cause of tides, while the sun's gravitational pull modifies the tidal pattern. Gravitational pull depends on mass and distance.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think gravity only pulls things 'down' toward the ground — they do not recognise that gravitational pull acts between any two masses, including between the moon and Earth's oceans.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If gravity is only 'down,' students cannot explain how the moon causes tides or how gravitational interactions govern the Earth-sun-moon system. The concept is extended in AC9S7U04 (Forces and Motion) where gravitational force is explored in terms of mass dependence.
teacher_glossary.response: Ask: if gravity only pulls down, how does the moon affect our oceans from space? The question exposes the limitation of 'gravity = down' and opens the door to gravity as a pull between any two masses.

teacher_glossary.definition: A push or pull acting on an object, measured in newtons (N). Forces are vector quantities — they have both magnitude (size) and direction. Multiple forces can act on an object simultaneously, and their combined effect determines whether the object's motion changes.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think of force as a single push or pull rather than recognising that multiple forces act simultaneously on every object — they identify the 'obvious' force (a hand pushing) but omit others (friction, gravity, normal force).
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If students identify only one force, they cannot construct complete force diagrams or determine whether forces are balanced or unbalanced. Every subsequent node depends on identifying all forces acting — the hinge_reason for Node 1 identifies force diagram errors as propagating into every later node.
teacher_glossary.response: For every scenario, require students to identify and name all forces before drawing. Use a checklist: gravity? normal force? friction? applied force? air resistance? The checklist builds the habit of checking for forces beyond the obvious one.

sub_terms.definition: A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction. Forces are vectors — a 10 N force pushing right is different from a 10 N force pushing left. Vectors are represented as arrows where length shows magnitude and the arrowhead shows direction.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students treat force arrows as labels (pointing at the object) rather than vectors showing direction and relative size — arrow length and direction carry no meaning in their diagrams.
sub_terms.response: Give students two force diagrams for the same scenario — one with correct vector arrows, one with random arrow sizes. Ask which correctly shows the forces and why. The comparison makes vector meaning explicit.

sub_terms.definition: The size or strength of a force, measured in newtons (N). In a force diagram, magnitude is represented by the length of the arrow — a longer arrow means a stronger force.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students draw all force arrows the same length regardless of the forces' actual relative sizes — the diagram looks neat but carries no quantitative information about which forces are stronger.
sub_terms.response: Give numerical force values and require arrow lengths to be proportional. A 20 N force arrow should be twice the length of a 10 N force arrow. Practice with a ruler builds the convention.

sub_terms.definition: The way a force acts — up, down, left, right, or at an angle. Direction determines whether forces add together (same direction), cancel out (opposite directions), or produce a change in direction (at an angle).
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students draw force arrows starting from the wrong point on the object or pointing away from the correct direction — particularly for normal force (drawn downward instead of upward) and friction (drawn in the direction of motion instead of opposing it).
sub_terms.response: For each force, ask: which direction does this force act? Start the arrow at the object's centre and point it in the direction the force pushes or pulls. Check: does friction oppose motion? Does normal force push away from the surface?

sub_terms.definition: The support force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it, acting perpendicular to the surface. For an object on a horizontal surface, the normal force acts upward and is equal in magnitude to the gravitational force when forces are balanced.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students omit normal force from diagrams — they draw gravity pulling down but nothing pushing up, even when the object is stationary on a surface. Or they confuse normal force with applied force.
sub_terms.response: Ask: if gravity pulls this book down, why doesn't it fall through the table? The table pushes back — that's normal force. Require students to draw both gravity and normal force for every object resting on a surface.

teacher_glossary.definition: A diagram showing all forces acting on an object as vector arrows, with correct relative magnitude and direction. Force diagrams are reasoning tools — they are how students identify whether forces are balanced or unbalanced and predict the resulting motion. Also called free body diagrams.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students treat force diagrams as illustrations rather than reasoning tools — they draw arrows decoratively without using the diagram to determine whether forces are balanced and what the motion outcome should be.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Force diagrams are the reasoning tool used across all subsequent nodes. Students with imprecise or decorative diagrams cannot correctly identify balanced or unbalanced states, predict motion changes, or distinguish mass from weight. The Node 1 hinge_reason identifies force diagram errors as propagating into every subsequent node.
teacher_glossary.response: After drawing every force diagram, require students to answer: are the forces balanced or unbalanced? What will happen to the object's motion? The diagram-to-prediction chain makes the diagram a reasoning tool rather than an illustration.

teacher_glossary.definition: Forces acting on an object that are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, resulting in no change to the object's motion. An object with balanced forces either stays stationary or continues moving at constant velocity — balanced does not mean 'no forces acting.'
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think balanced forces mean no forces are acting — rather than equal and opposite forces cancelling out. This misconception makes them unable to explain why an object moving at constant velocity has balanced forces.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The 'balanced = no forces' misconception propagates into every subsequent node. Students who hold it cannot explain constant velocity, cannot correctly predict motion states from force diagrams, and cannot understand Newton's First Law. It is the most common and persistent misconception in this standard.
teacher_glossary.response: Present an object moving at constant velocity (e.g. car at steady speed). Ask: are forces acting? Draw the force diagram. Students discover that driving force and friction are equal and opposite — balanced forces with motion. The constant velocity case directly contradicts the 'balanced = no forces = no motion' chain.

sub_terms.definition: The state of an object when all forces acting on it are balanced — the net force is zero. An object in equilibrium may be stationary or moving at constant velocity.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think equilibrium means nothing is happening — no forces, no motion. They miss that equilibrium is a dynamic state where forces are present but balanced, and motion can be occurring.
sub_terms.response: Present an object at constant velocity and a stationary object side by side. Both are in equilibrium — both have balanced forces. The moving example breaks the 'equilibrium = stillness' association.

sub_terms.definition: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity, unless acted upon by an unbalanced force. At Year 7, this is understood qualitatively as the principle underlying balanced force reasoning.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students state Newton's First Law but cannot apply it — they recite the definition without connecting it to force diagram analysis or using it to predict motion states from balanced/unbalanced assessments.
sub_terms.response: After every force diagram analysis, ask: does Newton's First Law predict the motion you identified? The repeated connection between the law and the diagram builds application rather than recitation.

sub_terms.definition: Movement at unchanging speed in an unchanging direction. An object at constant velocity has balanced forces — the driving force equals the opposing force. Constant velocity is the key case that disproves the misconception that balanced forces mean no motion.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think constant velocity requires a continuous applied force with no opposing force — they do not recognise that constant velocity means balanced forces, not zero forces.
sub_terms.response: Ask: a car drives at a steady 60 km/h on a flat road. Is there friction? Is there a driving force? Are they equal? The car is moving — but forces are balanced. This is the case that breaks the misconception.

teacher_glossary.definition: Forces acting on an object that do not cancel out — the net force is not zero. Unbalanced forces cause a change in motion: the object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction. Any change in motion requires an unbalanced force.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students apply unbalanced force reasoning only to obvious acceleration (car speeding up) and miss that slowing down and changing direction also require unbalanced forces — they do not recognise deceleration or turning as force-caused changes.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If unbalanced forces only cause speeding up, students cannot explain braking, falling, turning or projectile motion using force reasoning. The generalisation — any change in motion requires an unbalanced force — is what makes force reasoning universally applicable.
teacher_glossary.response: Present four scenarios: starting, stopping, speeding up, turning. For each, ask: is the motion changing? Draw the force diagram. Identify the unbalanced force. The range of scenarios builds the generalisation that any motion change = unbalanced force.

teacher_glossary.definition: A change in an object's velocity — its speed, direction, or both. At Year 7, acceleration is understood qualitatively: a greater unbalanced force produces a greater acceleration, and a greater mass produces a smaller acceleration for the same force.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think acceleration means only 'speeding up' — they do not recognise slowing down (deceleration) or changing direction as forms of acceleration.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If acceleration is only speeding up, students cannot explain braking as negative acceleration or turning as directional acceleration. The qualitative force-mass-acceleration relationship assessed at Node 5 requires understanding all three forms of acceleration.
teacher_glossary.response: Present three cases: a car speeding up, a car braking, and a car turning a corner at constant speed. Ask: is the velocity changing in each case? All three are acceleration — the definition is 'change in velocity,' not 'going faster.'

sub_terms.definition: A decrease in speed — acceleration in the direction opposite to the object's motion. Deceleration is not a separate concept from acceleration; it is acceleration where the unbalanced force opposes the direction of travel.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think deceleration is fundamentally different from acceleration — a separate category rather than acceleration in the opposite direction. This prevents them from applying force-acceleration reasoning to braking scenarios.
sub_terms.response: Draw force diagrams for a car speeding up and a car braking. In both cases, an unbalanced force causes acceleration — the only difference is the direction of the net force relative to motion. Deceleration is acceleration, just in the opposite direction.

teacher_glossary.definition: The attractive force between any two objects that have mass. On Earth, gravitational force pulls objects toward the centre of the Earth. The strength of gravitational force depends on mass — more massive objects experience a greater gravitational force. Extends gravitational pull from AC9S7U03 with the mass-dependence relationship.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think gravitational force is a property of Earth alone rather than a force between any two masses — they cannot extend the concept to the moon, other planets, or objects in space.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If gravity is an Earth-only property, students cannot reason about gravitational force on other planets, between celestial bodies, or in the mass-force relationship. The concept is extended quantitatively (F=ma) in AC9S10U05 (Newton's Laws) — students who treat gravity as Earth-specific cannot access the universal treatment.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare gravitational force on Earth, Moon and Mars for the same object. Mass stays constant; gravitational force changes. Ask: what determines how strong gravity is? The comparison across bodies forces the generalisation beyond Earth.

sub_terms.definition: The strength of the gravitational field at a location, measured in N/kg. On Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 N/kg (often rounded to 10 N/kg at Year 7). Weight = mass × gravitational field strength. Different planets and moons have different values of g.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students treat g as a fixed universal constant rather than a value that varies by location — they cannot explain why weight changes on different planets while mass does not.
sub_terms.response: Give students a table of g values for Earth, Moon and Mars. Calculate the weight of the same object at each location. Ask: what changed? What stayed the same? The calculation makes the variable nature of g concrete.

teacher_glossary.definition: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg). Mass is a property of the object itself — it does not change with location. Mass determines how much gravitational force an object experiences and how much it resists acceleration.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students conflate mass and weight — using the terms interchangeably, saying 'I weigh 60 kilograms' rather than 'my mass is 60 kg and my weight on Earth is about 600 N.'
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Mass/weight confusion propagates directly into AC9S10U05 (Newton's Laws of Motion). F=ma is meaningless if students conflate mass and weight — they substitute weight for mass in calculations, producing systematically wrong answers. The distinction must be functional, not just definitional.
teacher_glossary.response: Compare the same object on Earth and on the Moon: mass is identical (same amount of matter), weight changes (different gravitational force). Ask: which measurement stays the same regardless of where you are? The location-change test makes the distinction functional.

teacher_glossary.definition: The gravitational force acting on an object, measured in newtons (N). Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg). Unlike mass, weight changes with location because gravitational field strength varies between planets, moons and other bodies.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students define weight correctly but revert to treating it as mass in practice — they calculate weight correctly when prompted but use 'weight' to mean 'mass' in everyday discussion and unstructured problems.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Definitional knowledge without functional application means the distinction collapses under assessment pressure. Students who can define weight but default to mass/weight conflation in practice will make systematic errors in force calculations.
teacher_glossary.response: In every force problem involving gravity, require students to calculate weight explicitly using W = mg before proceeding. The habitual calculation builds functional use of the distinction, not just definitional recall.

teacher_glossary.definition: A scientific model explaining the behaviour of matter in terms of tiny particles. The four key ideas are: all matter is made of particles; particles are in constant motion; particles are attracted to each other; the spacing, motion and attraction between particles differ across states and determine observable properties.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students cannot reliably reproduce all four components of the model — they remember particles and spacing but omit motion or attraction, producing an incomplete model that cannot explain properties like viscosity or changes of state.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The four-component model is the explanatory framework for all subsequent nodes. Students who hold an incomplete model treat particle diagrams decoratively rather than as reasoning tools — they draw diagrams without using them to explain properties. This is the Node 1 hinge.
teacher_glossary.response: Use a four-point checklist every time students explain a property: particles — spacing — motion — attraction. Require all four to be addressed in every particle theory explanation. The checklist builds completeness as a habit.

teacher_glossary.definition: A visual representation of how particles are arranged, spaced and moving in a substance. Particle diagrams are reasoning tools — they should be used to explain observable properties (density, compressibility, viscosity) and predict behaviour, not just to label states of matter.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students draw particle diagrams as decorative illustrations rather than using them as explanatory tools — the diagram is added after the explanation rather than being the basis for it.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If particle diagrams are decorative, students cannot use the particle model to explain properties or predict behaviour. The pattern-recognition built through using diagrams as reasoning tools in Node 2 is what enables the explanatory move in Node 3. Node 2's hinge_reason identifies this directly.
teacher_glossary.response: Reverse the task order: give students a particle diagram and ask them to predict the substance's properties from the diagram before revealing what the substance is. This makes the diagram the starting point for reasoning rather than an afterthought.

teacher_glossary.definition: The three common forms in which matter exists — solid, liquid and gas — each characterised by a distinct arrangement, motion and attraction between particles. The state of a substance determines its observable properties and can change when energy is added or removed.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students identify states by macroscopic appearance only ('hard = solid, wet = liquid, invisible = gas') without connecting to the particle-level differences that define each state.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If states are defined by appearance rather than particle arrangement, students cannot explain why some substances defy expectations (e.g. liquid mercury is a shiny metal, glass is an amorphous solid). The particle-level definition is what makes the model explanatory rather than descriptive.
teacher_glossary.response: Present substances that challenge appearance-based classification: mercury (liquid metal), glass (solid but transparent), steam (invisible gas). For each, ask: what state is this? How do you know from the particle model, not from how it looks?

sub_terms.definition: A state of matter in which particles are closely packed in a fixed, regular arrangement with strong attractions between them. Particles vibrate in fixed positions but do not move freely. Solids have a definite shape and volume.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think particles in a solid are completely still — not vibrating. This prevents them from explaining how solids expand when heated or how energy input leads to melting.
sub_terms.response: Use an animation or vibrating model to show particles in a solid oscillating in fixed positions. Ask: if the particles were completely still, what would happen if we added heat energy? The vibration is what increases when energy is added.

sub_terms.definition: A state of matter in which particles are close together but not in fixed positions — they can slide past each other. Attractions between particles are weaker than in solids but still significant. Liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students confuse the liquid and gas particle models — drawing liquid particles widely spaced (like a gas) or gas particles close together (like a liquid). The spacing distinction is what they miss.
sub_terms.response: Place solid, liquid and gas particle diagrams side by side and ask students to rank by spacing. Liquids are close to solids in spacing but differ in arrangement (not fixed). The comparison clarifies the liquid's intermediate position.

sub_terms.definition: A state of matter in which particles are widely spaced, move rapidly in all directions, and have very weak attractions between them. Gases have no fixed shape or volume — they expand to fill their container.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think gas particles move slowly or stay in one area of the container — they do not connect the rapid, random motion of gas particles to the macroscopic property of filling any container.
sub_terms.response: Use a perfume-in-a-room demonstration or animation: spray perfume at one end and it reaches the other end. Ask: how did the scent particles get there? The rapid random motion of gas particles explains the observation.

teacher_glossary.definition: Characteristics of a substance that can be observed or measured without changing the substance's chemical composition — such as density, compressibility, viscosity, melting point and boiling point. Physical properties are explained at the particle level by differences in particle arrangement, motion and attraction.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students list physical properties without connecting them to the particle model — they treat properties as standalone facts rather than as consequences of particle behaviour that can be explained and predicted.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Using particle theory explanatorily — not just descriptively — is directly prerequisite for AC9S7U06 (Pure Substances and Mixtures). Selecting and justifying separation techniques requires explaining property differences at the particle level. Node 3's hinge_reason identifies this explicitly.
teacher_glossary.response: For every physical property, require a particle-level explanation: what about the particles causes this property? Use the format: '[Property] occurs because the particles are [arrangement/motion/attraction description].' The sentence frame forces the explanatory connection.

sub_terms.definition: The mass per unit volume of a substance (how much matter is packed into a given space). At the particle level, density depends on how closely particles are packed and the mass of individual particles. Solids are generally denser than liquids, which are denser than gases.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think density is the same as weight ('heavy things are dense') without recognising that density is mass per unit volume — a small piece of lead is denser than a large piece of wood, even though the wood may be heavier.
sub_terms.response: Compare a small steel ball and a large wooden block. Which is denser? Which is heavier? The two answers differ — density is about how tightly packed the mass is, not total mass.

sub_terms.definition: How much a substance can be squeezed into a smaller volume. Gases are highly compressible because particles are widely spaced; liquids and solids are nearly incompressible because particles are already close together.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students state that gases are compressible without explaining why in terms of particle spacing — or they think liquids should be compressible because they 'flow.'
sub_terms.response: Use a syringe demonstration: seal the end and push — air compresses, water does not. Ask: what is different about the particle spacing in each that explains this? The physical demonstration grounds the particle explanation.

sub_terms.definition: A measure of how easily a liquid flows — how much it resists flowing. At the particle level, viscosity depends on the strength of attraction between particles and how easily they can slide past each other. High viscosity (honey) = strong attractions; low viscosity (water) = weaker attractions.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students describe viscosity as 'thickness' without connecting it to particle attractions — they think viscosity is about how much stuff is in the liquid rather than how strongly particles attract each other.
sub_terms.response: Compare honey and water: both are liquids, but honey flows much more slowly. Ask: what is different about the particles? The answer is attraction strength, not particle number or size.

sub_terms.definition: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, driven by the random motion of particles. Diffusion occurs in liquids and gases and is faster in gases because particles move more rapidly and are more widely spaced.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students describe diffusion as particles 'wanting' to spread out — attributing purpose or intention to particle movement rather than understanding it as a statistical consequence of random motion.
sub_terms.response: Use a drop of food colouring in water. Ask: do the dye particles 'know' where to go? No — each particle moves randomly. But because there are more dye particles in one spot, random movement naturally spreads them out. Purpose-free explanation.

teacher_glossary.definition: The transformation of a substance from one state of matter to another — caused by adding or removing energy. During a change of state, energy changes the arrangement and motion of particles rather than raising the temperature. The substance's chemical composition does not change.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students confuse temperature change with state change — they think energy input always raises temperature, and cannot explain why temperature plateaus during melting or boiling even though energy is still being added.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: The temperature-plateau concept is directly assessed in success criteria. If energy input always means temperature rise, students cannot interpret heating curves, cannot explain why ice stays at 0°C while melting, and cannot distinguish the energy that changes arrangement from the energy that changes temperature.
teacher_glossary.response: Analyse a heating curve together. At the plateau: ask 'is energy still being added?' (yes) 'is temperature rising?' (no) 'so where is the energy going?' (changing particle arrangement, not temperature). The contradiction between energy input and constant temperature is the key teaching moment.

sub_terms.definition: The change of state from solid to liquid, occurring when energy input increases particle motion until particles can overcome their fixed arrangement and begin to slide past each other. Requires energy input.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students describe melting as particles 'breaking apart' rather than overcoming fixed positions — they think the particles separate widely rather than maintaining close spacing while gaining freedom to move.
sub_terms.response: Compare particle diagrams for solid and liquid — particles are still close together in both states. Ask: what changed? Arrangement and motion changed; spacing barely changed. Melting is about freedom of movement, not separation.

sub_terms.definition: The change of state from liquid to solid, occurring when energy is removed and particle motion decreases until particles lock into fixed positions. Freezing is the reverse of melting and releases energy.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students do not recognise freezing as the reverse of melting or that it releases energy — they think freezing just 'happens when it's cold' without connecting it to energy removal and particle behaviour change.
sub_terms.response: Present melting and freezing as mirror processes: melting adds energy and frees particles; freezing removes energy and locks particles. Ask: if melting requires energy input, what does freezing require? The symmetry makes the energy direction clear.

sub_terms.definition: The change of state from liquid to gas, occurring at the surface of a liquid when particles with enough energy escape the attractions of neighbouring particles. Unlike boiling, evaporation occurs below boiling point and only at the surface. Requires energy input.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students confuse evaporation with boiling — they think evaporation only happens at boiling point rather than occurring at any temperature when surface particles have sufficient energy.
sub_terms.response: Ask: why does a puddle dry up on a warm day when the temperature is well below 100°C? The answer — some surface particles have enough energy to escape — distinguishes evaporation from boiling.

sub_terms.definition: The change of state from gas to liquid, occurring when gas particles lose enough energy that attractions between them cause them to cluster together. Condensation is the reverse of evaporation and releases energy.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students think condensation is water appearing 'from nowhere' — they do not connect the water droplets on a cold glass to water vapour in the air losing energy and changing state.
sub_terms.response: Breathe on a cold window or place a cold can on a table. Ask: where did the water come from? It was already in the air as invisible water vapour — the cold surface removed energy, causing the gas particles to condense into visible liquid.

sub_terms.definition: Energy must be added (input) for changes from more ordered to less ordered states (melting, evaporation, sublimation) and is released (output) for changes from less ordered to more ordered states (freezing, condensation). During state changes, energy changes particle arrangement rather than temperature.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students cannot consistently identify whether energy is added or removed for each state change — they guess rather than reasoning from the particle model about whether particles are gaining or losing freedom of movement.
sub_terms.response: Arrange all state changes on a diagram from most ordered (solid) to least ordered (gas). Arrows going right require energy input; arrows going left release energy. The visual pattern replaces guessing with reasoning.

sub_terms.definition: A graph showing temperature change over time as a substance is heated or cooled. Sloping sections show temperature change within a state; flat sections (plateaus) show state changes where added energy changes particle arrangement rather than temperature.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students cannot interpret plateau regions on heating curves — they expect temperature to rise continuously and think flat sections mean the heater is broken or no energy is being added.
sub_terms.response: Give students a heating curve and ask them to label each section: what state is the substance in? Is it changing state or changing temperature? What is the energy doing in the flat sections? The section-by-section analysis builds interpretation skill.

teacher_glossary.definition: A substance composed of only one type of particle — either a single element or a single compound. At the particle level, a pure substance has uniform composition throughout: every particle is identical. Pure substances have fixed, predictable physical properties (e.g. a specific melting point).
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students classify substances as 'pure' based on appearance or common usage ('pure water from the tap,' 'pure orange juice') rather than applying the particle-level definition — one type of particle throughout.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If 'pure' means 'clean' or 'natural,' students cannot distinguish pure substances from homogeneous mixtures at the particle level — and technique selection in Nodes 3–5 depends on knowing what type of mixture is present. This is the Node 1 hinge.
teacher_glossary.response: Present tap water, distilled water and filtered river water. Ask: which is a pure substance? Students must apply the particle-level test (one type of particle only), not appearance. Distilled water is the only pure substance — even 'clean' tap water contains dissolved minerals.

teacher_glossary.definition: A substance composed of two or more different types of particles that are physically combined but not chemically bonded. The components of a mixture retain their individual properties and can be separated by physical methods. Mixtures may be homogeneous (uniform throughout) or heterogeneous (visibly different regions).
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students think mixtures must be visibly mixed — they classify clear, uniform solutions (saltwater, cordial) as pure substances because the components are not visible. The homogeneous/heterogeneous distinction is the gap.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If solutions look pure, students misidentify them and select inappropriate separation techniques. The particle-level distinction — different types of particles mixed together vs one type of particle — is the only reliable test and is directly assessed in success criteria.
teacher_glossary.response: Show particle diagrams for a pure substance and a solution side by side. Both look uniform to the eye, but the diagrams show different particle types in the solution. Ask: how can you tell these apart without a particle diagram? (Answer: test physical properties — a solution has different boiling point, density, etc.)

sub_terms.definition: A mixture that is uniform throughout — the different particle types are evenly distributed, so every sample has the same composition. Solutions are the most common type. Homogeneous mixtures cannot be distinguished from pure substances by appearance alone.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students confuse homogeneous mixtures with pure substances because both look uniform — the 'homo = same' prefix reinforces the misconception that it's the same as pure.
